paper_b.title: Yet another proof of Brooks' theorem

metadata.description: Both papers prove Brooks' theorem. Paper A (Hladky-Kral'-Schauz) gives an algebraic proof via the Alon-Tarsi polynomial method, reducing Brooks to the existence of an orientation of $G$ whose even/odd Eulerian-subgraph counts differ; this also delivers the stronger list-degree-colorability and degree-paintability versions. Paper B (Rabern) gives a short purely combinatorial proof on a minimal counterexample, extracting an induced $K_\Delta$ or odd cycle $T$ from $G - M$ for a maximal independent set $M$ and gluing two non-adjacent vertices of $N(T)$. Same target theorem, fundamentally different proof techniques — a clean alternative-proof (AP) pair.

matches.explanation: Brooks' theorem itself. Paper A states the classical form (TP409.3, cited from Brooks 1941: connected graphs of max degree $\Delta$ are $\Delta$-colorable unless they are odd cycles or $K_n$) and a strengthened list-and-paintable corollary (CP409.1). Paper B states the contrapositive form (TP413.1: $\chi(G)=\Delta+1\ge 4$ forces $K_{\Delta+1}\subseteq G$). The two formulations are logically equivalent statements of Brooks' theorem; we cluster the cited classical version and the paper-A list/paint corollary against paper B's main statement. Note: TP409.3 is `external`-origin in paper A (cited classical result) while CP409.1 is paper-origin; pairing them together with TP413.1 captures the same theorem regardless of formulation.

Paper A's algebraic main theorem (TP409.4) is strictly stronger than Brooks: it asserts list degree colorability and degree paintability for any non-Gallai-tree connected graph, with the classical Brooks dichotomy emerging as the $\Delta$-regular special case (via CP409.1). Paper B (TP413.1) only proves the chromatic-number form. Same target object (a colorability statement on connected graphs with the same exceptional family — odd cycles and complete graphs / Gallai trees) but different strength and framing, so analogous rather than exact.

The two proofs of Brooks' theorem. They occupy the same role (the proof step that closes the theorem) but use disjoint machinery: PP409.3 builds an orientation of $G$ in which every vertex has out-degree $\ge 1$ and the even/odd Eulerian-subgraph counts differ, then invokes the Alon-Tarsi theorem and its paintability variant; PP413.1 uses a minimal counterexample, a maximal independent set $M$, an induced $K_\Delta$ or odd cycle $T\subseteq G-M$, and a gluing of two non-adjacent vertices of $N(T)$. This is the essence of the AP relationship — same theorem, fundamentally different proof technique. The composite `proof_step` DAGs are listed only for context; we deliberately avoid emitting individual L2 step matches because the steps share no common structure.

Composite L2-vs-L2 alignment of the two proofs' inner step DAGs, attached to the parent proof match (PP409.3 vs PP413.1). The six steps of paper A's algebraic proof (reduce to orientation existence; apply structural lemma to obtain even cycle; build vertex ordering by contracting $C$; orient $C$ cyclically and the rest backward; enumerate Eulerian subgraphs and compare parities; conclude via Alon-Tarsi and paintability theorems) and the five steps of paper B's combinatorial proof (set up minimal counterexample and deduce $\Delta$-regularity; extract $T = K_\Delta$ or odd cycle from $G-M$; rule out $K_{\Delta+1}-xy$; pick non-adjacent $x,y\in N(T)$ and form glued $H$; color $H$ and extend to $T$) have no step-by-step correspondence. We record the cluster correspondence at low confidence to make the proof-decomposition contrast explicit; the only shared move is `case_split`/`contradiction_setup` flavor-of-argument, not specific content.
Even Eulerian subgraph — a definition specific to the algebraic (Alon-Tarsi) proof technique. Paper B's combinatorial proof never invokes orientations or Eulerian subgraphs.
Odd Eulerian subgraph — symmetric counterpart of DP409.1, also specific to the algebraic proof. No analogue in paper B.
$(k+1)$-paintability via the Paint-Correct game. Paper B works only with ordinary chromatic number $\chi$, never with paintability or list colorings.

Gallai tree — the structural exceptional family characterising when degree-list-colorability fails. Paper B uses only the classical Brooks exceptional family ($K_n$ and odd cycles) implicitly via $K_{\Delta+1}$, and never names the more general Gallai-tree concept.
List degree colorability — the strengthened conclusion of paper A's main theorem. Paper B does not address list colorings at all.
Degree paintability — also exclusive to paper A's stronger statement; no counterpart in paper B.

Structural lemma: every connected non-Gallai-tree graph contains an induced even cycle with at most one chord. This lemma is the technical heart of paper A's proof, supplying the cycle around which the orientation is built. Paper B never produces an induced even cycle and has no analogous structural lemma.
DFS-style vertex ordering lemma (folklore). Used by paper A to construct the linear order in which the orientation is defined. Paper B does not order the vertices; its argument is global on $G$.

Proof of the structural lemma (LP409.1) — the five-claim argument finding the shortest cycle inducing neither a complete graph nor an odd cycle. Internal to paper A's technique; no counterpart in paper B.
Proof of the DFS-ordering lemma. Internal to paper A; nothing analogous in paper B.
Claim 1 of the structural-lemma proof: existence of a cycle inducing neither a complete graph nor an odd cycle. Specific to paper A's structural argument.
Claim 2: no universal vertex on the shortest such cycle of length $\ge 5$. Specific to paper A.
Claim 3: each vertex of the shortest such cycle is incident with at most one chord. Specific to paper A.
Claim 4: the shortest such cycle is even. Specific to paper A.
Claim 5: the shortest such cycle has at most one chord. Specific to paper A.
